mechanism: The Allied victory in World War II made the Big Three the arbiters of Germany's postwar fate, which the Potsdam conference settled.
Nazi Germany's aggression and unconditional surrender created the defeated state whose occupation, reparations and borders Potsdam set.
Yalta fixed occupation zones, reparations principles and Polish questions that Truman, Stalin and Attlee then refined at Potsdam.
Potsdam agreements set four-power occupation zones and joint governing principles for Germany, structuring Allied rule from 1945 to 1949.
Soviet occupation zone fixed at Potsdam became the base of the German Democratic Republic, founded in East Germany in 1949.
Western occupation zones fixed at Potsdam were merged into the Federal Republic of Germany, founded in West Germany in 1949.
Potsdam deadlock over reparations and Poland's borders deepened Soviet-Western mistrust that hardened into the Cold War.
Crusaders of the First Crusade captured Jerusalem in 1099 and established the Latin kingdom there under Godfrey of Bouillon.
Seljuk conquest of Syria and Palestine after Manzikert seized Jerusalem and prompted the Byzantine appeal to Pope Urban II.
Seljuk victory at Manzikert in 1071 crippled Byzantine power and led Alexios I to seek Western military aid.
Saladin's conquest of Jerusalem in 1187, after the kingdom's army was destroyed at Hattin, prompted the Third Crusade to recover it.
Knights Templar were founded in Jerusalem around 1119 with royal backing to protect pilgrims on the kingdom's roads.
Alfonso VI's Christian advances in Iberia, including the capture of Toledo in 1085, prompted Andalusi taifa rulers to summon Almoravid forces.
Rigid Almoravid rule provoked Ibn Tumart's movement, which launched the Almohad revolt that overthrew the dynasty in Morocco and Iberia.
Genoese fleet support under the 1261 Treaty of Nymphaeum let Nicaean forces retake Constantinople, ending the Latin Empire.
Muhammad's prophetic movement unified the Arabian tribes into a single Muslim community, which the caliphate inherited after his death in 632.
Abu Bakr's Ridda Wars forced rebellious Arabian tribes back under Medinan authority, securing the caliphate's core territory.
Rashidun armies under Umar defeated the Sasanian Empire at al-Qadisiyyah and Nahavand, conquering Persia by 654.
Rashidun forces defeated Byzantine armies at Yarmuk in 636 and went on to conquer Syria.
Amr ibn al-As led a Rashidun army that invaded and conquered Byzantine Egypt between 639 and 642.
After the First Fitna civil wars, Muawiya founded the Umayyad Caliphate in 661, ending the Rashidun succession.
Philip II's centralizing policies, heavy taxation and Spanish troops in the Netherlands provoked the Dutch revolt that began the war in 1568.
Protestant spread through the Low Countries gave Dutch rebels religious grievances and sustained the revolt against Spanish Catholic rule.
Counter-Reformation enforcement under Philip II, including heresy persecution and the Inquisition, intensified Dutch resistance and rebellion.
Renaissance humanism revived ancient texts and mathematics and encouraged direct empirical study, providing methods used by early scientists.
Overseas voyages of the Age of Discovery brought new botanical, astronomical and geographical data that challenged classical authorities.
Hulagu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, established the Ilkhanate in Persia in 1256 as a subordinate khanate of the Mongol Empire.
Hulagu's Ilkhanate army sacked Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid Caliphate and bringing Iraq under Mongol rule.
Ilkhanate expansion into Syria under Hulagu led to the Mamluk victory at Ain Jalut in 1260 that halted Mongol westward advance.
After the Ilkhanate collapsed in 1335, its Iraqi and Persian territories fragmented, and the Jalayirid Sultanate emerged from the succession struggles.
During the War of the Polish Succession, Spanish Bourbon forces under Charles of Bourbon seized Naples and Sicily from Austria in 1734, creating the kingdom.
Aksumite armies under King Kaleb invaded Himyar in the early sixth century, ending its independence and bringing Yemen under Aksumite control.
The Soviet Union's 1924 national delimitation created the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic as one of its constituent republics.
Turkestan ASSR's territory and Soviet-run administration were reorganized in 1924 to form the core of the Uzbek SSR.
Bukharan People's Soviet Republic, a Soviet client state, was absorbed into the Uzbek SSR when it was founded in 1924.
Khorezm People's Soviet Republic was merged into the Uzbek SSR in 1924 after Soviet forces had established control over it.
Printing presses standardized punctuation across printed books, and Aldus Manutius introduced the semicolon in Venice in 1494.
Renaissance humanist interest in classical Greek and Latin grammar encouraged printers to adopt new punctuation marks like the semicolon.
Chinese gunpowder technology in the thirteenth century enabled explosive devices that were buried or placed in siege and field warfare.
Early gunpowder bombs developed in China around 1221 gave military engineers the explosive principle later used in buried land mines.
Laser interferometry, developed after 1960, gave LIGO the precision needed to detect the tiny strain of a gravitational wave in 2015.
Digital computers allowed LIGO scientists to filter noise and run matched-filter searches that identified the 2015 gravitational wave signal.
Ottoman sultans created the Janissary corps from conscripted Christian boys, making it the standing infantry of the Ottoman state.
Bernard of Clairvaux's preaching at Vezelay in 1146 persuaded Louis VII and many nobles to take the cross for the Second Crusade.
Napoleon chose to seek a decisive battle against the Austro-Russian armies in Moravia in 1805, and his deception and maneuvers forced them to attack at Austerlitz.
Hitler's Wehrmacht launched the offensive of May 1940 through the Ardennes, breaking French and British defenses and forcing France to surrender.
Post-Impressionist painters such as Cezanne, Gauguin and Van Gogh extended Impressionist color and light while rejecting its naturalism.
Post-Impressionist experiments with form and color by Cezanne and Gauguin provided a foundation for the modernist break with academic representation.
Van Gogh's emotionally charged color and distortion directly inspired German Expressionist painters in the early 1900s.
The Russian Orthodox metropolitan moved his seat to Moscow in the 1320s, giving the princes of Moscow religious prestige that aided their rise.
The death of King Louis II at Mohacs in 1526 left Hungary and Bohemia vacant, and the Habsburgs claimed both crowns through Ferdinand I.
Ferdinand II's Catholic recatholicization policies in Bohemia and the Habsburg claim to Bohemia triggered the Thirty Years' War.
Habsburg claims to Hungary after Mohacs drew the Ottoman Empire into prolonged wars along the Danube frontier.
Viking raids and settlement destroyed the Pictish and Northumbrian power structures, letting Kenneth MacAlpin unite Picts and Scots around 843.
Reinforced concrete allowed modernist architects to build long spans and thin cantilevers, shaping the modern architectural style.
Radio wireless telegraphy created the need for detectors and amplifiers, which Fleming and De Forest met with the early vacuum tube in 1904-1906.
Vacuum tubes provided the switching elements of the first electronic digital computers, such as ENIAC in 1945.
Limitations of vacuum tubes in size, power and reliability motivated Bell Labs to develop the transistor as their replacement.
The Achaemenid Persian Empire created the satrapy system, dividing its territory into provinces ruled by satraps appointed by the king.
Assyrian imperial pressure on the Zagros peoples pushed the Median tribes to unite under a single kingship in the seventh century BC.
Medes allied with Babylonians under Nabopolassar and sacked Nineveh in 612 BC, ending the Neo-Assyrian Empire.
The Median-Babylonian alliance that toppled Assyria let Nabopolassar establish the Neo-Babylonian Empire over the old Assyrian lands.
Hitler ordered Operation Citadel in July 1943, with Nazi Germany's panzer divisions attacking the Kursk salient to regain the initiative in the East.
After the German defeat at Stalingrad, the Wehrmacht lacked the strength of earlier years and sought a decisive summer offensive at Kursk.
The Soviet defensive victory at Kursk destroyed much of Germany's remaining offensive armour, reducing forces available to defend France in 1944.
Soviet forces under Zhukov and Konev launched the April 1945 offensive that encircled and captured Berlin.
Hitler refused to surrender and ordered the defense of Berlin, making the city the site of the final battle in Europe.
Soviet capture of Berlin placed the city inside the Soviet zone, which later shaped the four-power occupation of Germany.
Growth of Huguenot Protestantism in France after 1555 created the confessional tensions that the Catholic royal court and Parisian mobs turned into massacre in 1572.
The birth of Jesus in Bethlehem began the life and ministry from which the Christian movement emerged in the first century.
The Great Depression after 1929 deepened unemployment and social conflict in Spain, weakening the moderate coalitions that had founded the 1931 Republic.
Polarization over the Republic's reforms and the political violence of 1934-1936 led conservative generals to rise against it, starting the Spanish Civil War.
Theban rulers of the Seventeenth Dynasty waged war against the Hyksos, and Ahmose I completed their expulsion to found the New Kingdom.
Rivalries and military reforms among the Warring States produced the Qin state that conquered the rest and unified China in 221 BC.
Louis-Napoleon's coup of December 1851 and plebiscite ended the French Second Republic and proclaimed the Second Empire in 1852.
The 1848 revolutions and fear of socialism convinced many French voters to back Louis-Napoleon as a strong order-restoring leader.
Napoleon III joined Britain against Russia in the Crimean War to win diplomatic prestige and assert French leadership in Europe.
Napoleon III's rivalry with Prussia and his declaration of war in July 1870 led to the Franco-Prussian War and the Sedan defeat.
The capture of Napoleon III at Sedan in September 1870 collapsed the Second Empire and led to the proclamation of the French Third Republic.
Edison's telegraph and telephone transmitter work in 1877 led directly to the tinfoil phonograph that recorded and played back sound.
The phonograph's cylinder and disc recording lineage fed directly into the commercial phonograph record introduced around 1887.
The 1789 federal government created Congress, which required a permanent Capitol building, and the 1790 Residence Act set the seat in Washington.
Independence from Britain created a new national government that needed a federal legislative building and capital.
The Holocaust revealed the consequences of unchecked state power, prompting Europeans to draft a binding charter of individual rights.
Nuremberg trials established principles of crimes against humanity that the Council of Europe drew on when drafting the convention.
Rome's victory at Zama in 201 BC rewarded Masinissa with rule over Numidia, creating the Numidian kingdom under Roman favor.
During the Second Punic War, Masinissa switched sides to Rome, which secured the Numidian kingdom's emergence from the Massylian and Masaesylian tribes.
Saxon migrations into southern Britain during the Migration Period created the settlements from which the kingdom of Wessex grew.
